nameStory: The wayfaring-tree earned its name from its habit of growing along roadsides and paths throughout Europe, where it became a familiar sight to travelers on their journeys. Early botanists noticed how this sturdy shrub seemed to follow human pathways, making it a reliable companion for wayfarers walking from village to village.
description: Wayfaring-tree is a vigorous deciduous shrub that can grow quite large, sometimes reaching tree-like proportions up to 15 feet tall. It's actually a European native that has found its way into New England landscapes, belonging to the same family as elderberries. This robust plant produces showy white flower clusters in spring followed by colorful berries that change from red to black as they ripen.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves with prominent veins and a distinctive wrinkled, velvety texture on top that feels almost like soft leather when you run your fingers across the surface

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped white flower clusters about 3-4 inches across that bloom in late spring, with tiny individual flowers packed tightly together like a natural bouquet

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Berries that start bright red and gradually turn black, often with both colors present in the same cluster, creating a striking two-toned effect

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, upright shrub with multiple sturdy stems that can become quite thick and tree-like with age, often spreading wider than it is tall

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish bark on younger stems that becomes slightly furrowed on older, thicker branches

habitat: In New England, wayfaring-tree is most commonly found in cultivated landscapes, parks, and naturalized areas near human habitation. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and often establishes itself along roadsides, woodland edges, and disturbed areas where it can receive partial to full sunlight.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters emerge in late spring, creating showy displays that attract various pollinators. New leaves unfurl with their characteristic wrinkled texture becoming most apparent.
seasonality.summer: Berries develop and begin their color transition from green to red, while the distinctive textured leaves remain the best identification feature throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Berries complete their transformation to black, and leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, though fall color is not particularly showy.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's sturdy structure, and you can identify it by its opposite branching pattern and any remaining dried fruit clusters.

funFact: The berries on a single cluster can be three different colors at once - green, red, and black - as they ripen at slightly different rates, creating natural rainbow clusters that look almost too perfect to be real!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other viburnums, but the wrinkled, velvety leaf texture is unique among New England viburnums - if the leaves feel like soft leather, you've found wayfaring-tree.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name including 'tree,' this plant is technically a shrub, though it can grow large enough to seem tree-like. As a European native, it's not part of New England's natural ecosystem but has adapted well to the region's climate.
compareHints: Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones. It also tends to grow larger and more robustly than most of its native cousins, and its berries show that characteristic red-to-black color progression that's less pronounced in other local viburnums.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
